title: Socket Programming
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of socket programming and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—socket—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study socket programming with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you build network-facing code that handles timeouts, untrusted responses, and partial failure. In this lesson, focus on socket and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Network calls can fail or stall even when request code is correct. Use the standard HTTP client, validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and apply bounded retries only where safe. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect socket with serversocket before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Socket
items.text: Network calls can fail or stall even when request code is correct. Use the standard HTTP client, validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and apply bounded retries only where safe.

items.title: ServerSocket
items.text: Network calls can fail or stall even when request code is correct. Use the standard HTTP client, validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and apply bounded retries only where safe.

items.title: Client-server exchanges
items.text: Network operations can fail, stall, or return untrusted data even when local code is correct. Validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and restrict retries to operations where repeating the request is safe. Apply that reasoning specifically to client-server exchanges and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Reading and writing network streams
items.text: A stream pipeline describes transformations over a source. Intermediate operations are lazy; a terminal operation triggers work, and stream instances should not be reused after a terminal operation.

items.title: Connection cleanup
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Separate address metadata from opening connections and sending network traffic. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: extend the example for socket programming to validate input and report a useful failure state. Keep network activity optional and use explicit timeouts before making a real request.
